source_read: PDF PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Anthony_1994_ComparativeEpidemiologyDependence.pdf (scanned, OCR text layer), pp. 244-268: text pp. 244-265 read in full from the OCR text; every number used checked on rendered pages (pp. 245-248, 251, 254, 256, 259, 261-265, including Tables 2, 4 and 5); reference list pp. 266-268 not needed.

claims.overstatement: None. One small inexactness: 'in the same survey' does not quite hold for tobacco; the 31.9% divides NCS tobacco dependence, assessed in a 55% subsample (4,414) and asking only about daily smoking, by tobacco-use prevalence from the 1991 NHSDA, which is why it has no standard error (pp. 248, 251). The magnitude's '(no SE)' is right.
claims.note: All Anthony numbers confirmed on the page images: 8,098; 82.4%; 46.3% (SE 1.1); 4.2% (0.3); 9.1% (0.7); tobacco 31.9% (no SE), heroin 23.1% (5.6), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), alcohol 15.4% (0.7) (Table 2, p. 251); men 12.0% (1.1), women 5.5% (0.7) (Table 5, p. 259; also p. 264). Recomputed: 4.2/46.3 = 9.07%; 9.1 +/- 1.96 x 0.7 = 7.7 to 10.5, as the claim's editors' calculation says; 6.2/51.7 = 12.0% and 2.3/41.0 = 5.6% (printed 5.5, rounding of unrounded inputs). Use was counted from a single occasion, so 'even once' is right (p. 248). The limitations sentence matches the source: dependence assessed only after several occasions of use (p. 248); 15-24-year-olds had just entered the main risk period (p. 262) with many years at risk left (p. 264); incomplete reporting of dependence problems would attenuate the proportion dependent among users (p. 263); deaths give an undercount and forgotten or casual use an overcount (p. 264). Not in the claim: the authors say overall rates change little when institutional residents are included, though perhaps not for groups with high incarceration (p. 265); and the earlier ECA survey gave close to 20% DSM-III abuse or dependence among people who had used cannabis more than five times (p. 263), which shows how much the figure depends on the denominator.

anchors.extracted: Stratified multistage area probability sample of people aged 15-54 in the noninstitutionalized civilian population of the 48 coterminous states, including students in campus housing; fieldwork 14 September 1990 to 6 February 1992.

anchors.locator: Method and Materials, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (continued from p. 245)
anchors.extracted: Overall response rate 82.4%, 8,098 participants; CIDI administered by 158 interviewers after 7 days of study training, with no training in psychopathology or psychopharmacology.

anchors.locator: Diagnostic Assessment of Alcohol and Other Drug Dependence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: DSM-III-R dependence from CIDI questions read by trained lay interviewers and scored by computer: at least 3 of 9 Criterion A manifestations plus Criterion B (at least one month, or repeatedly over a longer period).

anchors.locator: Diagnostic Assessment (continued), 1st paragraph; Assessment of Tobacco Use and Dependence; Analysis Procedures, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Dependence questions asked only after at least several occasions of use (as few as six assumed possibly sufficient); use prevalence counts anyone with at least one occasion; dependence among users = dependence prevalence divided by use prevalence; tobacco dependence assessed in a subsample of 4,414 (55%) and tobacco use taken from the 1991 NHSDA, so no standard errors for tobacco.

anchors.locator: Table 2, Cannabis, Tobacco, Alcohol, Cocaine and Heroin rows
anchors.extracted: Cannabis: lifetime dependence 4.2% (SE 0.3), lifetime use 46.3% (1.1), dependence among users 9.1% (0.7). Dependence among users: tobacco 31.9% (no SE), alcohol 15.4% (0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), heroin 23.1% (5.6). Weighted, n = 8,098 (tobacco n = 4,414).

anchors.locator: Results > Drug Use and the Transition to Drug Dependence, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: 46.3% had used cannabis at least once and 9.1% of them had developed dependence; cannabis ranked low on dependence among users despite being the most used drug after alcohol and tobacco (sentence continues on p. 255).
Men: use 51.7% (1.3), dependence 6.2% (0.6), dependence among male users 12.0% (1.1); women: 41.0% (1.5), 2.3% (0.3), 5.5% (0.7).

anchors.locator: Discussion > Transition From Drug Use to Drug Dependence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: ECA: close to 20% DSM-III abuse or dependence among people who had used cannabis more than five times; NCS: a large majority of users never became dependent; authors see a strong possibility that some participants with dependence under-reported their problems, which would attenuate the proportion dependent among users.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Future Directions for Research and Other Implications, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cross-sectional design relying on retrospective self-report; leaves out people who have died (an undercount where dependence carries a high risk of death) and long-forgotten or casual use not worth mentioning (an overcount: mildly affected people neglected).

anchors.locator: Discussion > Future Directions for Research and Other Implications, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Sampling frame limited to noninstitutionalized residents; authors cite evidence that overall rates change little when institutional residents are included, though possibly not for groups with high drug-related incarceration.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim correctly says the age groups are by age at interview, not age at first use, and attributes the before-17 point to studies the authors cite.
claims.note: Table 4 figures confirmed on the page image (p. 256): dependence among people who had used cannabis 15.3% (SE 2.3) at 15-24, 8.1% (0.7) at 25-34, 8.5% (1.3) at 35-44 and 3.1% (1.5) at 45-54 (labelled 45+ in a sample aged 15-54). Recomputed from the same rows: 5.6/36.5 = 15.3%, 5.0/61.6 = 8.1%, 4.4/52.1 = 8.4% (printed 8.5), 0.8/25.5 = 3.1%. The authors' own reading (p. 264): 15-24-year-olds had a comparatively high proportion dependent although they had many years at risk left, possibly because early-onset users (before 17) seem at higher risk of drug problems even after adjustment for duration of use (Anthony & Petronis, 1993; Robins & Przybeck, 1985), so the figure may fall as later starters join. Not in the claim: the authors also suggest that age differences may reflect birth cohort, period and drug availability, and that drug-related deaths deplete older groups (p. 261), which bear on the low 3.1% at 45-54 as much as on the high figure at 15-24.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Comparative Epidemiology of Tobacco, Alcohol, and Other Drug Dependence, paragraphs beginning 'These relationships between age' and 'The first general observation'
anchors.extracted: Age differences in dependence may reflect variation in availability or involvement across birth cohorts, periods or life stages; drug-related deaths progressively remove dependent people from older age groups.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Comparative Epidemiology of Tobacco, Alcohol, and Other Drug Dependence, paragraph beginning 'The second general epidemiologic observation'
anchors.extracted: Adolescence to age 34 is the main risk period for starting drug use and dependence; in 1990-92 the 15-24-year-olds had only just entered it.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Transition From Drug Use to Drug Dependence, paragraph beginning 'Notwithstanding these general observations'
anchors.extracted: 15-24-year-old users had comparatively high dependence for cocaine, alcohol and Schedule I drugs such as marijuana despite many years at risk remaining; early-onset illicit users (before 17) seem at higher risk of drug problems than later starters even after adjustment for duration of use (two cited studies); cumulative occurrence may later decline as later starters are added.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence checklist, editors' summary low, holds for the cannabis figures as for stimulants: national probability sample, 82.4% response, standardized CIDI applied identically across drug classes, design-based standard errors. The limits that matter for cannabis (noninstitutionalized frame; dependence asked only after several occasions; self-report; 1990-92 cannabis) are directness and interpretation, not risk of bias.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract gives only aggregates; 'transition' language invites a risk reading the cross-sectional ratio does not support; the 20-40% statement does not fit cocaine.

missed: The card was written for methamphetamine and has no finding for the cannabis values the two cannabis claims now rest on: Table 2 (p. 251) cannabis lifetime use 46.3% (SE 1.1) and dependence 4.2% (0.3), with 9.1% (0.7) among users; Table 4 (p. 256) dependence among users by age at interview 15.3% (2.3), 8.1% (0.7), 8.5% (1.3) and 3.1% (1.5); Table 5 (p. 259) men 12.0% (1.1) and women 5.5% (0.7); the text restates these on p. 254 (46.3% and 9.1%; 1 dependent for every 10 not, p. 255) and p. 264 (12% and 5.5%). All checked on the page images.

The authors' reading of the age pattern, used by the frequency and onset claim: 15-24-year-old users had comparatively high dependence for cocaine, alcohol and Schedule I drugs such as marijuana; early-onset illicit users (before 17) seem at higher risk of drug problems even after adjustment for duration of use, citing two studies; the figure may fall as later starters are added (p. 264); 15-24-year-olds had just entered the main risk period (p. 262); and age differences may reflect birth cohort, period and availability, with drug-related deaths depleting older groups (p. 261).

ECA and NCS lifetime prevalences of cannabis disorders were 4.4% and 4.2% (p. 258; DSM-III abuse or dependence against DSM-III-R dependence), and the ECA proportion among people who had used cannabis more than five times was close to 20% (p. 263): useful context for how much the 9.1% depends on the denominator.
